name: Hashimoto encephalopathy (SREAT)
aliases: steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis
encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroid disease

reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / neuro-endocrine reference literature
clinicalPearls: A rare steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with high titres of thyroid autoantibodies, particularly anti-thyroid-peroxidase (anti-TPO)
Presents with fluctuating encephalopathy, cognitive decline, seizures, myoclonus, psychiatric symptoms and stroke-like or tremulous episodes
Thyroid function is often normal or only mildly deranged, so the encephalopathy is not simply due to hypothyroidism
It is a diagnosis of exclusion, requiring careful ruling out of infective, metabolic, toxic, vascular and other autoimmune encephalitides
The presence of thyroid antibodies is a marker of autoimmunity rather than proof of a direct pathogenic role
Cerebrospinal fluid frequently shows a raised protein without infection, and the EEG commonly demonstrates non-specific slowing
The characteristic and often dramatic response to glucocorticoids for Hashimoto encephalopathy supports the diagnosis and guides treatment
reference.pathophysiology: The mechanism is incompletely understood but is thought to be an immune-mediated process affecting the brain in patients with autoimmune thyroid disease. Proposed mechanisms include autoimmune cerebral vasculitis or an antibody-mediated attack on shared neural and thyroid antigens, causing a non-vasculitic inflammatory encephalopathy. The anti-thyroid antibodies are considered a serological marker of the underlying autoimmune tendency rather than directly neurotoxic, and the frequently normal thyroid hormone levels indicate that the encephalopathy is distinct from the metabolic effects of hypothyroidism. The condition's steroid responsiveness is consistent with an inflammatory, immune-driven process.
additionalDifferentials: Autoimmune (antibody-mediated) encephalitis such as anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis
additionalInvestigations: Anti-thyroid-peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin antibody titres with thyroid function tests
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis including protein, cell count and infective studies
Autoimmune and paraneoplastic encephalitis antibody panel to exclude alternatives
MRI of the brain to exclude structural, vascular and inflammatory lesions
redFlags: Status epilepticus or rapidly progressive coma
Features suggesting an alternative treatable encephalitis or CNS infection
Rapidly progressive dementia raising concern for prion disease
An underlying occult malignancy suggesting a paraneoplastic process
reference.prognosis: Most patients improve substantially with corticosteroid therapy, and the outlook is generally favourable, though relapses occur and some patients have residual cognitive deficits.
pitfalls: Assuming thyroid antibodies confirm the diagnosis without excluding other encephalitides
Attributing the encephalopathy to hypothyroidism and correcting thyroid hormone alone
Missing an alternative antibody-mediated or infective encephalitis
Withholding a corticosteroid trial once mimics have been reasonably excluded
Failing to monitor for relapse after treatment
references: Neurology reference literature on steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis
management: Treat with high-dose corticosteroids as first-line therapy, to which the encephalopathy characteristically responds rapidly
Escalate steroid-refractory or relapsing disease to intravenous immunoglobulin, plasma exchange, or steroid-sparing immunosuppressants such as azathioprine or rituximab
Correct coexisting thyroid dysfunction with levothyroxine where the patient is hypothyroid
Control seizures and myoclonus with antiseizure medication as needed
Exclude infective, metabolic, toxic, vascular, and other autoimmune encephalitides before and alongside treatment, as this is a diagnosis of exclusion
Monitor cognitive and clinical recovery, surveilling for relapse as corticosteroids are tapered
Manage jointly through neurology and endocrinology
